entities.summary:
Charles Montagu, 1st Duke of Manchester (c. 1662 – January 20, 1722), was a pivotal British aristocrat and diplomat whose career spanned the tumultuous transition from the late Stuart monarchy to the establishment of the Hanoverian dynasty. A staunch Whig, his political and diplomatic service was crucial in advancing British interests and securing the Protestant succession during an era marked by intense European power struggles and domestic factionalism. His elevation to dukedom reflected his significant contributions to the state, particularly in bolstering alliances against French hegemony and navigating the complex currents of post-Glorious Revolution politics.

Montagu's diplomatic career began with his appointment as ambassador to Venice (1697–1698), where he engaged in intricate negotiations reflecting Britain's growing European influence. His most significant foreign posting was as Ambassador to France (1699–1701), a critical period leading up to the War of the Spanish Succession, where he navigated the complexities of Louis XIV's court and the contentious issue of the Spanish succession. He later served as Secretary of State for the Southern Department (1708–1710) under Queen Anne, overseeing diplomatic relations with Catholic Europe, before returning to Venice as Ambassador Extraordinary (1707–1708). He was instrumental in securing support for the Protestant succession and maintaining the balance of power in Europe against Bourbon expansionism.
